rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading begins the command to trust with fa; the other seven canonical readers use waw.
rows.anchor: فتوكل بالفاء، وباقي السبعة: بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired names mean the One who cannot be overcome and the One who shows mercy; trust in Him defeats enemies through might and brings aid through mercy. Tawakkul entrusts affairs to their capable owner.
rows.anchor: فهو يقهر أعداءك بعزته، وينصرك عليهم برحمته. والتوكل هو تفويض الأمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, understand the Prophet's rising as his rising for prayer.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين منهم ابن عباس، على أن المعنى حين تقوم إلى الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read taqallub as a verbal noun coordinated with the object in God seeing the Prophet; Janah ibn Hubaysh reads it as a present verb coordinated with يراك.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وتقلبك مصدر تقلب، وعطف على الكاف في يراك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada gloss those prostrating as people who pray.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة: في الساجدين: في المصلين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet's light passed through the loins of Adam, Noah, and Abraham until his emergence.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: في أصلاب آدم ونوح وإبراهيم حتى خرجت

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima understands God to see the Prophet standing and prostrating.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: يراك قائما وساجدا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternate gloss takes the Prophet's rising as private retreat by himself.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: يراك قائما وساجدا. وقيل: معنى تقوم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also says the Prophet's turning is his looking among those praying behind him, as in a report that he saw worshippers behind his back.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أيضا: المراد تقلب بصره فيمن يصلي خلفه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says prayer is the apparent sense, though Mujahid and Qatada allow all the Prophet's activities and movements among worshippers.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية أنه يريد قيام الصلاة، ويحتمل أن يريد سائر التصرفات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, and others take the prostrators as those praying with the Prophet; Ibn Abbas and Qatada also mean believers generally, described as prostrators.
rows.anchor: أي صلاتك مع المصلين، قاله ابن عباس وعكرمة وغيرهما

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says the phrase means the Prophet's movement among the prophets, like their movements.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير: أراد الأنبياء، أي تقلبك كما تقلب غيرك من الأنبياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari pictures the Prophet praying at night and discreetly checking his companions' worship and inner states; after night prayer was abrogated, he toured their homes and heard their devotional murmuring.
rows.anchor: طاف تلك الليلة ببيوت أصحابه لينظر ما يصنعون، بحرصه عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prostrators can mean worshippers, and the verse may describe God seeing the Prophet lead congregational prayer through standing, bowing, prostration, and sitting.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالساجدين: المصلون. وقيل: معناه يراك حين تقوم للصلاة بالناس جماعة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil reports asking Abu Hanifa whether congregational prayer appears in the Quran; Abu Hanifa cited this verse.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل، أنه سأل أبا حنيفة رضي الله عنه: هل تجد الصلاة في الجماعة في القرآن؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may also assure that no aspect of the Prophet's state is hidden when he rises and moves among worshippers while managing religious affairs.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن لا يخفى علي حالك كلما قمت وتقلبت مع الساجدين في كفاية أمور الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears what the Prophet says and knows his intentions and actions.
rows.anchor: إنه هو السميع لما تقوله، العليم بما تنوبه وتعمله

rows.speaker: الرافضة
rows.claim: The Rafidites argue that the Prophet's forefathers were believers, construing the verse as God transferring his spirit from one prostrator to another; they say all possible senses should be retained because none conflicts or prevails.
rows.anchor: وذهبت الرافضة إلى أن آباء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كانوا مؤمنين

rows.speaker: الرافضة
rows.claim: They also cite a prophetic report that the Prophet was passed through pure loins and wombs, and infer that disbelievers are impure.
rows.anchor: لم أزل أنقل من أصلاب الطاهرين إلى أرحام الطاهرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Abraham's address to Azar, father can mean uncle; Jacob's sons likewise called Ismail their father although he was their uncle.
rows.anchor: فلفظ الأب قد يطلق على العم، كما قالوا أبناء يعقوب له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address means Tell them, O Muhammad; the interrogative is for eliciting acknowledgment and establishing the point.
rows.anchor: أي قل يا محمد: هل أخبركم؟ وهذا استفهام توقيف وتقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The embedded question is governed by تنزل and suspends أنبئكم; once suspended, it conveys a statement about whom devils visit rather than a genuine request for information.
rows.anchor: والاستفهام إذا علق عنه العامل، لا يبقى على حقيقة الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afaak and athim are intensive forms meaning habitual liar and habitual sinner; the intended people are soothsayers.
rows.anchor: فأفاك أثيم: صيغتا مبالغة، والمراد الكهنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in yulqun may refer to devils listening for fragments of angelic speech to carry to soothsayers, or passing what they heard to those visited; aktharuhum can mean most devils lie.
rows.anchor: والضمير في يلقون يحتمل أن يعود إلى الشياطين، أي ينصتون ويصغون بأسماعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, yulqun can refer to soothsayers lending an ear to devils, or delivering heard words to people; in either reading most of the soothsayers lie.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يعود الضمير في يلقون على كل أفاك أثيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soothsayers may receive one true word heard from heaven and mix a hundred lies with it; the true word can mislead those who hear it.
rows.anchor: يتلقون من الشياطين الكلمة الواحدة التي سمعت من السماء، فيخلطون معها مائة كذبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no contradiction between calling every soothsayer habitually mendacious and saying most are liars: habitual liars can sometimes tell the truth, though they are mostly deceived.
rows.anchor: ولا تعارض بين قوله: كل أفاك، وبين قوله: وأكثرهم كاذبون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says repeated separation of the Quran's statements from nearby ones highlights them again and again, signaling God's special disapproval of the meanings involved.
rows.anchor: أريد التفريق بينهن بآيات ليست في معناهن، ليرجع إلى المجيء بهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing soothsayers' falsehood, the passage denies that the Quran is their speech: opponents had called the Quran poetry and the Messenger a soothsayer.
rows.anchor: نفي كلام القرآن، إذ كان بعض الكفار قال في القرآن: إنه شعر

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: When a man of Ali's family said poetry surged in his heart, Amr ibn Ubayd asked why he did not use it for harmless subjects.
rows.anchor: فقال: ما يمنعك منه فيما لا بأس به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The poets exempted from condemnation are identified as Hassan, Abdullah ibn Rawaha, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and others defending the Messenger.
rows.anchor: المراد بالمستثنين: حسان، وعبد الله بن رواحة، وكعب بن مالك، وكعب بن زهير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet urged Ka'b ibn Malik to satirize the opponents, saying such verse struck harder than arrows, and told Hassan that the Holy Spirit was with him.
rows.anchor: اهجهم فو الذي نفسي بيده لهو أشد عليهم من النبل

rows.speaker: عطاء بن يسار
rows.claim: Ata ibn Yasar and others say the poets Hassan, Ibn Rawaha, and Ka'b were distressed by the condemnation, told the Prophet, and the exception was then revealed at Medina.
rows.anchor: شق ذلك على حسان وابن رواحة وكعب بن مالك، وذكروا ذلك للرسول

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd specifies that remembering God much means that the poets remember Him in their poetry.
rows.anchor: وخص ابن زيد قوله: وذكروا الله كثيرا، فقال: أي في شعرهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says remembrance became their habit; Labid said God had replaced poetry with the better Quran.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: صار خلقا لهم وعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the permitted poets' vindication, the text threatens their unjust opponents with an unspecified terrible destination.
rows.anchor: توعد الظالمين هذا التوعد العظيم الهائل الصادع للأكباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Bakr recited the threat when appointing Umar, and the righteous early Muslims used it to admonish one another; in legal usage, the unjust here are unbelievers.
rows.anchor: ولما عهد أبو بكر لعمر رضي الله عنهما، تلا عليه: وسيعلم الذين ظلموا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says interpreting the unjust as unbelievers is a restrictive causal interpretation, characteristic of his Mu'tazilite position.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الظلم بالكفر تعليل، وكان ذكر قبل أن الذين ظلموا مطلق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Arqam, transmitting from Hasan, read منفلت with fa and two ta letters: wrongdoers hope to escape punishment but discover no route to safety.
rows.anchor: أي منفلت ينفلتون، بفاء وتاءين

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa treats أي منقلب as a verbal noun adjective modifying an omitted verbal noun; yanqalibun is its governing verb.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: أي منقلب مصدر نعت لمصدر محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author distinguishes conditional, interrogative, relative, adjectival, vocative, and vocative-link uses of ayya; al-Akhfash treats the vocative form as relative, while most grammarians treat it as a separate category.
rows.anchor: فأي تكون شرطية واستفهامية وموصولة، ووصفا على مذهب الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In قد علمت أي ضرب تضرب, ayya is interrogative, not an adjective describing an omitted verbal noun.
rows.anchor: فهي استفهامية، لا صفة لمصدر محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lexeme ردء means support or help: a supporting beam props a wall up, and Abu Ubayda glosses it as assistance; the cited verse fragment witnesses the word.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: العون، ويقال: ردأته على عدوه: أعنته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مقبوح means expelled or driven away, supported by the cited poetic line about being disgraced.
rows.anchor: المقبوح: المطرود، وقال الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ثوى means to stay or reside; two poetic citations use it, and الثوي denotes a resident guest.
rows.anchor: ثوى يثوي ثواء: أقام، قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words بطر and سرمد mean arrogance or tyranny and something lasting without end.
rows.anchor: البطر: الطغيان. السرمد: الدائم الذي لا ينقطع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan, Ata, and Ikrima say the whole surah is Meccan.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية كلها، قاله الحسن وعطاء وعكرمة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil identifies the passage beginning الذين آتيناهم الكتاب من قبله through لا نبتغي الجاهلين as Medinan.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: فيها من المدني الذين آتيناهم الكتاب من قبله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report places the surah's revelation between Mecca and al-Juhfa; Ibn Abbas locates that revelation at al-Juhfa during the Hijra.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بالجحفة، في خروجه عليه السلام للهجرة

rows.speaker: ابن سلام
rows.claim: Ibn Sallam says the promise that the Quran's prescriber will return him to a destination was revealed at al-Juhfa during the migration to Medina.
rows.anchor: نزل إن الذي فرض عليك القرآن لرادك إلى معاد، بالجحفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens by answering the prior surah's command to praise God and promise to show signs: the Quran is the greatest miracle and sign, though some say the book is the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الكتاب هو القرآن، وقيل: اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Netlu means either recite to Muhammad through Gabriel's recitation or recount; min nabaʾ means part of the story, while bil-haqq means truthfully or describes the story as clothed in truth.
rows.anchor: نتلوا: أي نقرأ عليك بقراءة جبريل، أو نقص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are specified because they are the people who benefit from the revelation.
rows.anchor: وخص المؤمنين لأنهم هم المنتفعون بالتلاوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's elevation means tyrannical arrogance and claiming divinity in Egypt; he divided the Copts into factions or assignments, enslaved Israelites, imposed tax on nonworkers, or set groups against each other.
rows.anchor: علا في الأرض: أي تجبر واستكبر حتى ادعى الربوبية والإلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oppressed party is the Children of Israel, and يستضعف may be an independent explanatory clause, a circumstantial clause, or an adjective describing the divided groups.
rows.anchor: والطائفة المستضعفة بنو إسرائيل. والظاهر أن يستضعف استئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce يذبح with gemination; Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin pronounce it with a single consonant.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يذبح، مضعفا وأبو حيوة، وابن محيصن: بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's being among the corrupters explains his tyranny and killing of sons, since this conduct is sheer corruption.
rows.anchor: إنه كان من المفسدين: علة لتجبره ولتذبيح الأبناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine intention to favor the oppressed is coordinated with the account of Pharaoh; treating it as a simultaneous circumstantial clause is weak, though imminent rescue makes the intention seem contemporaneous.
rows.anchor: ونريد: حكاية حال ماضية، والجملة معطوفة على قوله: إن فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's favor means rescuing the Israelites from Pharaoh and drowning him.
rows.anchor: وأن نمن: أي بخلاصهم من فرعون وإغراقه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says making the Israelites leaders means making them callers to good.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: دعاة إلى الخير

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the leaders are rulers, like the Quran's description of making people kings.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ولاة، كقولهم: وجعلكم ملوكا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets the leaders as prophets.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: أنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heirs inherit Pharaoh's rule and possessions; Ali says they were Joseph and his descendants, while Qatada also says they inherited Egypt and Syria.
rows.anchor: وعن علي، الوارثون هم: يوسف عليه السلام وولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read ونمكن in coordination with نمن; al-Aʿmash reads ولنمكن, construing it as purpose or as God's stated aim.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: ولنمكن، بلام كي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establishing the Israelites in the land means enabling them to enforce their command and control others in Egypt and Syria.
rows.anchor: والتمكين: التوطئة في الأرض، هي أرض مصر والشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read ونري with an accusative object; Abdullah, Hamza, and al-Kisai read ونرى with the following object nominative.
rows.anchor: وعبد الله، وحمزة، والكسائي: ونرى، مضارع رأى، ورفع ما بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Haman is named because he was Pharaoh's notable minister and an important unbelieving figure; they feared losing power and being destroyed by an Israelite child.
rows.anchor: وهامان: وزير فرعون وأحد رجاله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada understand God's revelation to Moses' mother as inspiration placed in the heart.
rows.anchor: إلهام وقذف في القلب، قاله ابن عباس وقتادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say the revelation came in a dream; Qutrub and others say an angel was sent, which the author regards as the apparent view because the passage promises return and prophethood.
rows.anchor: أو إرسال ملك، قاله قطرب وقوم، وهذا هو الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is consensus that Moses' mother was not a prophet; angelic communication to her would resemble angel visits or angelic conversations with ordinary people.
rows.anchor: وأجمعوا على أنها لم تكن نبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation apparently followed Moses' birth, requiring an omitted clause that she gave birth while fearing Pharaoh's infanticide; another view places it before birth.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا الإيحاء هو بعد الولادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The أن before suckling may be explanatory or a source-forming particle.
rows.anchor: وأوحينا، وأن تفسيرية، أو مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amr ibn Abd al-Wahid and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read ارضعيه with kasra on nun after irregular hamza deletion; Warsh transfers the hamza's fatha, the regular form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن عبد الواحد، وعمر بن عبد العزيز: أن ارضعيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear means fear of Pharaoh's spies and agents killing infants; casting Moses into the Nile is the commanded response. Al-Junayd reads this spiritually as handing over to God when mediated protection fails.
rows.anchor: فإذا خفت عليه من جواسيس فرعون ونقبائه الذين يقتلون الأولاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports differ on the length of Moses' nursing: three, four, or eight months.
rows.anchor: وزمان إرضاعه ثلاثة أشهر، أو أربعة، أو ثمانية، أقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yam is the Nile in Egypt; fear of drowning, loss, or capture is forbidden, and grief at separation is also forbidden; the promise reassures her of his survival and prophethood.
rows.anchor: واليم هنا: نيل مصر. ولا تخافي: أي من غرقه وضياعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ta-Ha account has already described the chest, its casting into the river, and its recovery, so those details need not be repeated.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم في سورة طه طرف من حديث التابوت ورميه في اليم

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi tells of a woman who, after a request to recite poetry, asked whether anything could be more eloquent than this verse, which combines two commands, two prohibitions, two statements, and two glad tidings.
rows.anchor: وقد جمع بين أمرين ونهيين وخبرين وبشارتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted sequence says she nursed Moses and cast him into the river; li-yakuna describes the eventual consequence of Pharaoh's family taking him, although they intended adoption and affection.
rows.anchor: واللام في ليكون للتعليل المجازي، لما كان مآل التقاطه وتربيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read huznan with both vowels open, a Quraysh dialect; several named readers use a damma on ha and sukun on za.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وحزنا، بفتح الحاء والزاي، وهي لغة قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A khatiʾ commits error deliberately, unlike a mukhtiʾ; the likely omitted sense is that Moses became their enemy and grief because they persisted in crimes and unbelief.
rows.anchor: والخاطئ: المتعمد الخطأ، والمخطئ: الذي لا يتعمده

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Pharaoh's family wronged themselves by taking Moses; other explanations blame killing Israelite children or raising their enemy.
rows.anchor: خاطئين على أنفسهم بالتقاطه. وقيل: بقتل أولاد بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and Haman are both associated with the troops although Haman had none, since army maintenance requires the minister to raise funds and the king to command and compel.
rows.anchor: إذ بالوزير تحصل الأموال، وبالملك وقهره يتوصل إلى تحصيلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading without hamza in خاطئين may reflect deleted hamza, which is likeliest, or derive from خطا يخطو, missing the right course.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: خاطيين، بغير همز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's household first considered killing Moses, fearing the Israelite child who might end their rule; God placed love of him in Asiya's heart, with reports of a light in the chest and Pharaoh's daughter loving him after his saliva cured her vitiligo.
rows.anchor: فألقى الله محبته في قلب آسية امرأة فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurrata is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning he is a comfort to the eye; reading it as the subject of لا تقتلوه is less plausible. Asiya said it would comfort both, and Pharaoh replied it would comfort her, not him.
rows.anchor: وذكر أنها لما قالت لفرعون: قرت عين لي ولك، قال: لك لا لي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asiya hoped Moses might benefit them or be adopted because signs of good appeared in him, including the light and healing of vitiligo.
rows.anchor: وأتبعت النهي عن قتله برجائها أن ينفعهم لظهور مخايل الخير فيه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the family did not realize Moses would ruin their kingdom; Mujahid says they did not realize he was their enemy; Ibn Ishaq says they did not realize God would do what He willed.
rows.anchor: قاله قتادة أو أنه عدو لهم، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes وهم لا يشعرون as God's words; the alternative makes it Asiya speaking of counselors who did not know she had persuaded Pharaoh, while al-Zamakhshari's parenthetical reading is less good than the surface syntax.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه من كلام الله تعالى. وقيل: هو من كلام امرأة فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart becoming فارغا means Moses' mother lost her composure when she heard he was with Pharaoh, overwhelmed despite the promise; she later regained calm through God's promise.
rows.anchor: وأصبح: أي صار فارغا من العقل، وذلك حين بلغها أنه وقع في يد فرعون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says her heart was empty of everything except remembering Moses.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: فارغا من كل شيء إلا من ذكر موسى

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik glosses فارغا as loss of reason.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: هو ذهاب العقل

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group says the heart was empty of patience; Ibn Zayd says she forgot God's promise and revelation from anxiety; Abu Ubayda says she was free of grief because Moses had not drowned, which the author finds unlikely.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: فارغا من الصبر

rows.speaker: أحمد بن موسى
rows.claim: Ahmad ibn Musa, transmitting from Abu Amr, reads فؤاد with waw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أحمد بن موسى، عن أبي عمرو فواد: بالواو

rows.speaker: فضالة بن عبيد
rows.claim: Fadala ibn Ubayd, Hasan, Yazid ibn Qutayb, and Abu Zurʿa read فزعا, denoting fear and anxiety.
rows.anchor: وقرأ فضالة بن عبيد، والحسن، ويزيد بن قطيب، وأبو زرعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also reads قرعا, from a bare or bald head, signifying that only Moses remained in her thought, or as a noun for the great blow of distress.
rows.anchor: وابن عباس: قرعا، بالقاف وكسر الراء وإسكانها

rows.speaker: بعض الصحابة
rows.claim: Some Companions read فزغا, meaning wasted away from anxiety, as witnessed by a line of Tulayha al-Asadi.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بعض الصحابة: فزغا، بالفاء مكسورة وسكون الزاي

rows.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
rows.claim: Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad reads فرغا with damma on both letters.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الخليل بن أحمد: فرغا، بضم الفاء والراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In إن كادت لتبدي, inna is the softened form of the emphatic particle and the laam distinguishes it.
rows.anchor: هي إن المخففة من الثقيلة، واللام هي الفارقة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A Kufan alternative treats إن as negative and laam as meaning except; the author says the pronoun in به apparently refers to Moses, with several grammatical accounts of the added ba or omitted object.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن نافية، واللام بمعنى إلا، وهذا قول كوفي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Moses' mother nearly cried out that he was her son when she put him in the river or saw waves tossing him.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كادت تصيح عند إلقائه في البحر وا ابناه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God steadied her heart through faith; al-Suddi says through protection, al-Sadiq through certainty, and Ibn Ata through revelation.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: بالإيمان. وقال السدي: بالعصمة. وقال الصادق: باليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stated aim is that she become one of those who believe God's promise will certainly come true; strengthening the heart is a metaphor for calm and firmness.
rows.anchor: والربط على القلب كناية عن قراره واطمئنانه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows فارغا to mean free of worry after she heard Pharaoh adopted Moses; she nearly revealed he was her son from joy, and God calmed her so she would trust His promise rather than Pharaoh's kindness.
rows.anchor: ويجوز: وأصبح فؤادها فارغا من الهم حين سمعت أن فرعون عطف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says al-Zamakhshari's reading departs from the exegetes' understanding; the omitted result of lawla is she would have exposed him, as in the similar construction in Joseph's story.
rows.anchor: وما ذهب إليه الزمخشري من تجويز كونه فارغا من الهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sister is told to follow Moses' trace and seek news of him; she secretly searched the streets and found the household looking for a wet nurse after he rejected nurses.
rows.anchor: قصيه: أي اتبعي أثره وتتبعي خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sister secretly searched the city; reports call her Maryam, Kulthama, or Kulthum, and the narrative omits that she followed Moses' tracks.
rows.anchor: فروي أنها خرجت في سكك المدينة مختفية، فرأته عند قوم

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani takes جنب as an adjective for an omitted place, meaning from a distant location.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني: جنب صفة لموصوف محذوف، أي عن مكان جنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations have the sister walk by the riverbank or say people did not realize she was following, was Moses' sister, or that he was their enemy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عن جانب، لأنها كانت تمشي على الشط

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says they did not realize Moses was their enemy.
rows.anchor: لا يشعرون أنه عدو لهم، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the sister looked at Moses as if she had no interest in him.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: معنى عن جنب: أنها تنظر إليه كأنها لا تريده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ on the vowels in جنب and بصرت; Nuʿman ibn Salim reads جانب, a synonym alongside جنابة and جناب.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النعمان بن سالم: عن جانب، والجنب والجانب والجنابة والجناب بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here haram means prevented; maradiʿ may mean wet nurses, breasts, or the act of nursing, and مِن قبل may mean from the outset or before the sister arrived.
rows.anchor: والتحريم هنا بمعنى المنع، أي منعناه أن يرضع ثدي امرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sister offers to guide them to a caring household with good upbringing; the plural implies they had tried several nurses. The pronoun apparently refers to Moses, though it might refer to the boy considered part of the king's household.
rows.anchor: ودل قوله: وحرمنا عليه المراضع، أنه عرض عليه جملة من المرضعات

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the people suspected she recognized the child and asked who he was; she evaded disclosure by saying only that her family would be loyal to the king.
rows.anchor: تأول القوم أن الضمير للطفل فقالوا لها: إنك قد عرفتيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted sequence has the sister bring the family to Moses' mother, who agrees to nurse him and he takes her breast.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف تقديره: فمرت بهم إلى أمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Pharaoh asked why the child accepted her breast when he rejected all others; she claimed uniquely good scent and milk, then received him and a daily dinar.
rows.anchor: إني امرأة طيبة الريح، طيبة اللبن، لا أوتى بصبي إلا قبلني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' mother could take him because the payment was enemy property and therefore permitted, not because she charged for nursing.
rows.anchor: وجاز لها أخذه لأنه مال حربي، فهو مباح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fulfilled return promise brought joy; tears of happiness are cool while a troubled person's eyes are hot, illustrated by Abu Tammam's verse.
rows.anchor: ودمع الفرح بارد، وعين المهموم حرى سخنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once God fulfilled His promise, Moses' mother knew he would become a prophet and messenger.
rows.anchor: لما أنجز تعالى وعده في الرد، ثبت عندها أنه سيكون نبيا رسولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return enabled her to know experientially that God's promise was true, though she had already known it would occur; most people do not know this purpose or the hidden decree.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: ولتعلم أن وعد الله حق دلالة على ضعف من ذهب

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says people do not know their own interests or the soundness of their eventual outcomes.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: لا يعلمون مصالحهم وصلاح عواقبهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and Muqatil also say people do not know that God had promised Moses' mother to return him.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك أيضا، ومقاتل: لا يعلمون أن الله وعدها رده إليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the city Moses entered as Memphis; reports place Pharaoh's visit there at noon or between evening prayers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هي منف

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says the city was Egypt itself; Moses had openly opposed Pharaoh and entered in disguise, wary and unseen.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: المدينة مصر بنفسها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Pharaoh had expelled Moses, who returned after years away when people had forgotten him; other reports suggest a festival, a palace exit, Heliopolis, Habin, or Alexandria.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: كان فرعون قد أخرجه من المدينة، فغاب عنها سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Talib reads حين with an accusative n and explains the unusual construction as treating the noun like a verb because it is followed by a past-tense clause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو طالب القارئ: على حين، بنصب نون حين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naim ibn Maysara reads يقتلان by assimilating the ta letters; the men may fight over religion or over a Copt forcing an Israelite to carry Pharaoh's firewood. The verb may describe the men or be circumstantial.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نعيم بن ميسرة: يقتلان. بإدغام التاء في التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelite is Moses' religious adherent, possibly the Samaritan; the Copt is his enemy, reportedly named Fatun. Demonstratives can stage absent past figures as present, as al-Mubarrad notes with a poetic example.
rows.anchor: هذا من شيعته: أي ممن شايعه على دينه، وهو الإسرائيلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read استغاثه as asking Moses for rescue; Sibawayh, Ibn Miqsam, and al-Zafarani read استعنانه as asking for aid.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فاستغاثه، أي طلب غوثه ونصره

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم يوسف بن علي بن جبارة
rows.claim: Ibn Jabbarah chooses Ibn Miqsam's aid-reading; Ibn Atiyya calls it a scribal error, but the author rejects that charge because Ibn Khalawayh and others transmit it from named readers.
rows.anchor: والاختيار قراءة ابن مقسم، لأن الإعانة أولى في هذا الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Copt threatened to burden Moses with carrying wood; enraged and physically strong, Moses struck him and he died. Other readings use لكزه or نكزه.
rows.anchor: فاشتد غضب موسى، وكان قد أوتي قوة، فوكزه، فمات

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Moses struck the Copt with his staff; other authorities say he used his fist.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: وكزه بعصاه وغيره قال: بجمع كفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject of فقضى may be Moses, God, or the blow understood from وكزه; Moses did not intend to kill, but the blow coincided with the man's appointed death, and he regretted it.
rows.anchor: وكان موسى لم يتعمد قتله، ولكن وافقت وكزته الأجل

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says a prophet may not kill unless commanded; Ka'b says Moses was twelve and killed accidentally because a blow ordinarily does not kill; al-Naqqash says this preceded prophethood.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن جريج: ليس لنبي أن يقتل ما لم يؤمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses calls the killing Satan's work because anger led to the fatal blow, names it a wrong against himself, and seeks forgiveness; he had no authorization to kill the man.
rows.anchor: وجعله من عمل الشيطان وسماه ظلما لنفسه واستغفر منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses follows Adam's language of self-wronging; the ba in بما أنعمت may be an oath with an omitted answer or depend on an omitted plea for protection through God's favor.
rows.anchor: وقد انتهج موسى عليه السلام نهج آدم عليه السلام إذ قال: ظلمنا أنفسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take لن أكون as a prayer with لن meaning لا, but the author says the correct view is that لن is not used in prayer.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن لن لا تكون في الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporting wrongdoers may mean accompanying Pharaoh, joining his ranks as his adopted son, or having earlier helped cause the killing; another view makes the blessing prophethood and limits support to God's allies.
rows.anchor: إما بصحبته لفرعون وانتظامه في جملته وتكثير سواده

rows.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
rows.claim: Scholars including Ata ibn Abi Rabah use this verse to prohibit helping or serving unjust rulers; Ata applies it when asked about a brother who writes for Khalid al-Qasri.
rows.anchor: واحتج أهل العلم بهذه الآية على منع معونة أهل الظلم وخدمتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' fear may concern being caught for the Copt's death, learning whether authorities knew, awaiting forgiveness or divine victory, or hoping his people would be guided or not betray him.
rows.anchor: فأصبح في المدينة خائفا من قبل القبطي أن يؤخذ به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إذا here marks sudden occurrence; بالأمس means the day before, with dialectal variation in its inflection, and يستصرخه means calling for help against another Copt, as a poem illustrates.
rows.anchor: وإذا هنا للمفاجأة، وبالأمس يعني اليوم الذي قبل يوم الاستصراخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent referent of له is the Israelite, whom Moses rebukes as a troublemaker for having caused the previous killing; an alternative takes the referent as the Copt, with the Israelite misunderstanding the rebuke.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الضمير في له عائد على الذي إنك لغوي مبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelite, mistaking Moses' intention, asks whether he means to kill him as he killed a man yesterday; rumor identified Moses as the killer and reached Pharaoh, who ordered Moses' death. Another reading makes the Israelite the one about to strike.
rows.anchor: وكان تعيين القائل القبطي قد خفي على الناس، فانتشر في المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading of يبطش has kasra on the ta for most readers and damma for Hasan and Abu Ja'far; لو after a preceding oath can introduce the conditional, with a poetic citation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يبطش، بكسر الطاء والحسن، وأبو جعفر: بضمها

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: The tyrant is one who kills without right; al-Shaʿbi says killing two people makes a person a tyrant, whom the verse contrasts with the righteous.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: من قتل رجلين فهو جبار، يعني بغير حق

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The man arriving from the far end of the city may be the believer from Pharaoh's family; al-Kalbi names him Jibril ibn Shamaun, al-Dahhak calls him Shamaun ibn Ishaq, and another view says he was someone else.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو مؤمن آل فرعون، وكان ابن عم فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yasʿa means he hastened; من أقصى المدينة and يسعى can both describe the man, though the latter can be circumstantial or the former attached to جاء. The author rejects al-Zamakhshari's restriction because Sibawayh allows a bare indefinite noun to take a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: يسعى: يشتد في مشيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ملأ are Pharaoh's state notables; يأتمرون means they consult, supported by al-Namr ibn Tawlab's poetry, while Ibn Qutayba glosses it as ordering one another, citing 2:233.
rows.anchor: إن الملأ، وهم وجوه أهل دولة فرعون، يأتمرون: يتشاورون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase لك متعلق either to an omitted statement that the man is Moses' adviser, as an explanation, or to الناصحين despite that word's adjectival construction; grammarians report three positions.
rows.anchor: ولك: متعلق إما بمحذوف، أي ناصح لك من الناصحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses trusted the man's warning, escaped his pursuers, and took an unfamiliar route alone while trusting and asking God to save him from the wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: وكان موسى لا يعرف ذلك الطريق، ولم يصحب أحدا، فسلك مجهلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawajjaha means he turned his face; tilqaʾ means toward the direction he faced, and the verbal noun is used adverbially.
rows.anchor: توجه: رد وجهه. وتلقاء: تقدم الكلام عليه في يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says three roads lay before Moses: he took the middle, pursuers took the others, and he went barefoot and hungry for eight nights, eating leaves.
rows.anchor: فأخذ موسى أوسطها، وأخذ طالبوه في الآخرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is that Moses did not know the route and asked God to guide him directly to safety; Ibn Abbas says God brought him to Midian as he walked without knowing the way.
rows.anchor: والظاهر من قوله: عسى ربي أن يهديني سواء السبيل، أنه كان لا يعرف الطريق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reports say Gabriel or another angel guided Moses, or he deliberately chose a safe road that happened to lead to Midian; Mujahid identifies it as the Midian road, Hasan as the path of guidance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هداه جبريل إلى مدين. وقيل: ملك غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reached the water of Midian; warada can mean reaching or entering, and the water was said to be a well. Umma is a large group, and عليه means at its bank or edge.
rows.anchor: ولما ورد ماء مدين: أي وصل إليه، والورود بمعنى الوصول إلى الشيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others say the women kept their sheep from the water because they feared the stronger shepherds; Qatada says they kept people away from the sheep, and al-Zajjaj says they avoided crowding.
rows.anchor: تذودان، قال ابن عباس وغيره: تذودان غنمهما عن الماء خوفا من السقاة الأقوياء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya takes من دونهم to mean the women stood before the crowd relative to Moses; al-Zamakhshari says they were in a lower place than the shepherds.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: The women may have been shielding their faces from men's gaze; al-Farra says they restrained the flock from scattering and gives their names as Abra and Sabura.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: تحبسانها عن أن تتفرق

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says asking ما خطبكما is appropriate for someone afflicted, oppressed, needing compassion, or facing an unusual matter; al-Zamakhshari derives it from the object of a pursuit.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والسؤال بالخطب إنما هو في مصاب، أو مضطهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' question shows it is permissible to speak with an unrelated woman when a need arises; the sisters lacked a hired worker and waited for shepherds to finish, since they could not draw water or compete with men.
rows.anchor: وفي سؤاله عليه الصلاة والسلام دليل على جواز مكالمة الأجنبية فيما يعن

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammar has a rare reading with kasra on خ, asking who their husband was and why he did not water for them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ شمر: بكسر الخاء، أي من زوجكما؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Musarrif reads لا نسقي with damma on nun; readers vary whether the shepherds return with their flocks or drive the flocks back. The raʿaʾ readings vary, and al-Bahr rejects al-Zamakhshari's claim that its kasra plural is a regular pattern.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مصرف: لا نسقي، بضم النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their father being an elderly man explains why they water the flock themselves and appeals to Moses for help.
rows.anchor: وأبونا شيخ كبير: اعتذار لموسى عن مباشرتهما السقي بأنفسهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses watered the two women's flock for their sake; reports say he alone lifted a well cover normally requiring seven to one hundred men, drew a bucket for forty, or pushed through the crowd.
rows.anchor: فسقى لهما: أي سقى غنمهما لأجلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses acted in hope of reward despite travel hardship and hunger; reports describe his belly showing green from leaves and the sole of his foot wearing away, yet he still helped them.
rows.anchor: كل ذلك رغبة في الثواب على ما كان به من نصب السفر وكثرة الجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women's answer fits Moses' question: they were weak and modest, unable to compete with men, and waited until shepherds left; their watering was permissible by Arab and Bedouin custom, especially under necessity.
rows.anchor: بأنا امرأتان ضعيفتان مستورتان، لا نقدر على مزاحمة الرجال

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says the shade Moses sat beneath was a tree; other reports identify it as a samura or a roofless wall, or say he turned his back to the sun.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود: ظل شجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes take Moses' plea that he is poor for whatever good God sent down as an indirect request for food; the word means bestow, and al-Zamakhshari says فقير carries the sense of asking.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: تعرض لما يطعمه، لما ناله من الجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively Moses declares spiritual poverty despite earlier worldly wealth, gratefully preferring rescue from oppressors; Hasan says he asked for more knowledge and wisdom.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يريد، أي فقير من الدنيا لأجل ما أنزلت إلي من خير الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted sequence has the daughters quickly tell their father what happened; he sends one to summon Moses. Which daughter is left unspecified, perhaps the elder or one of twins born half a day apart.
rows.anchor: في الكلام حذف، والتقدير: فذهبتا إلى أبيهما من غير إبطاء في السقي

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar says the woman walked modestly with the sleeve of her dress covering her face; the phrase على استحياء functions circumstantially.
rows.anchor: قال عمر بن الخطاب: قد سترت وجهها بكم درعها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Most say the girls' father was the prophet Shuaib; Hasan says he was Shuaib's nephew Marwan, and Abu Ubayda names him Harun.
rows.anchor: والجمهور: على أن الداعي أباهما هو شعيب عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views identify the girls' father as an unrelated righteous man or their uncle, the sheep owner, whom she called father because he filled that role.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو رجل صالح ليس من شعيب ينسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offer to pay Moses for watering shows Shuaib's generosity in compensating a worker even when the worker did not seek payment.
rows.anchor: في ذلك ما كان عليه شعيب من الإحسان والمكافأة لمن عمل له عملا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses went with the woman based on her report, evidence that a woman's report can be relied upon as in transmission of reports.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دليل على اعتماد أخبار المرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses recounts his departure from Egypt and its cause; Shuaib reassures him that God accepted his plea for rescue or tells him he has escaped, then offers food as hospitality rather than payment for watering.
rows.anchor: وقص عليه القصص: أي ما جرى له من خروجه من مصر، وسبب ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The daughter who proposes hiring Moses means him to tend and water their sheep; she cites his strength in lifting the stone and drawing the bucket and his trustworthiness when he asked her to guide him from behind.
rows.anchor: ووصفتْه بالقوة: لكونه رفع الصخرة عن البئر وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combining competence and trustworthiness completes the requirements for a caretaker; the daughter explains these traits by his strength and modest conduct.
rows.anchor: إذا اجتمعت الكفاية والأمانة في القائم بأمر، فقد تم المقصود

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud names three perceptive people: Shuaib's daughter, Joseph's master who hoped Joseph would be useful, and Abu Bakr in selecting Umar.
rows.anchor: أفرس الناس ثلاثة: بنت شعيب وصاحب يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports the lawfulness of hiring; the author says this was permitted in every religious law and essential to people's dealings, rejecting Ibn Aliya and al-Asamm's contrary view as against consensus.
rows.anchor: وفي قولها: استأجره، دليل على مشروعية الإجارة عندهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuaib wants Moses as a son-in-law because of his strength and trust, detachment from worldly life, reliance on God, and flight from unbelievers.
rows.anchor: رغب شعيب في مصاهرته، لما وصفته به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warsh and Ahmad ibn Musa, transmitting from Abu Amr, omit the hamza in أنكحك إحدى.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ورش، وأحمد بن موسى، عن أبي عمرو: أنكحك احدى، بحذف الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent wording gives the wali a role in contracting marriage, unlike Abu Hanifa's allowance in some cases for an adult competent woman to contract her own marriage.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: أن أنكحك، أن الإنكاح إلى الولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports a wali offering his ward to a prospective husband, as Umar did; Malik and al-Shafiʿi allow a father to marry his virgin daughter without consultation, while Abu Hanifa requires her consent once adult.
rows.anchor: وفيه دليل على عرض الولي وليته على الزوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer that a marriage is valid only with the terms nikah or tazwij; Rabiʿa, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, Abu Ubayd, and Dawud hold that view.
rows.anchor: وفيه دليل على قول من قال: لا ينعقد إلا بلفظ التزويج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Offering one of the two unnamed daughters is a proposal, not a contract, because Shuaib says he intends to marry; the bride must be identified at contract, and the hire's start term is not yet fixed.
rows.anchor: وإحدى ابنتي: مبهم، وهذا عرض لا عقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse apparently permits marriage in exchange for service; al-Shafiʿi and his companions and Ibn Habib accept this, while al-Zamakhshari's inference that Shuaib had other daughters from هاتين is rejected because it points to the two women just seen.
rows.anchor: والظاهر من الآية جواز النكاح بالإجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: على أن تأجرني is circumstantial from the agent or object in أنكحك; تأجرني means you work for me, its second object is omitted, and حجج may be an adverb or an object meaning eight years of tending.
rows.anchor: على أن تأجرني في موضع الحال من ضمير أنكحك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second object of تأجرني is omitted and understood as yourself; eight حجج can be a temporal adverb or, as al-Zamakhshari says, the object denoting eight years of herding.
rows.anchor: ومفعول تأجرني الثاني محذوف تقديره نفسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completing ten years is an unrequired gift; Shuaib promises not to burden Moses with either the longer term, intrusive oversight, or tasks outside the agreement, and promises fair or generally righteous treatment if God wills.
rows.anchor: فإن أتممت عشرا فمن عندك: أي هو تبرع وتفضل لا اشتراط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' that is between us statement fixes their mutual agreement at eight years; either eight or ten may be completed, and he cannot be wronged by demands beyond the agreed term.
rows.anchor: ذلك الذي عاهدتني وشارطتني قائم بيننا جميعا لا نخرج عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hasan and al-Abbas from Abu Amr read أيما without the second ya; Abdullah's variant inserts ما after الأجلين, and al-Zamakhshari says the standard placement broadens the choice while the variant stresses resolve to complete a term.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، والعباس، عن أبي عمرو: أيما، بحذف الياء الثانية

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abu Haywa and Ibn Qutayb read فلا عدوان with kasra on the first letter.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة، وابن قطيب: فلا عدوان، بكسر العين

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says mentioning both periods is deliberate even though demanding more than the longer term would be wrong: it makes completing the shorter seem as good as the longer.
rows.anchor: قد علم أنه لا عدوان عليه في أتمهما، ولكن جمعهما

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says injustice appears with the shorter term if Moses is forced to complete ten; the reply compares this with demanding more than ten, which would plainly be unjust.
rows.anchor: تصور العدوان إنما هو في أحد الأجلين الذي هو أقصر
